origin_region: Shizuoka · Kawane, Honyama and Tenryū; Kyoto · Uji; Fukuoka · Yame
cultivar: Yabukita; Kōshun, Yamakai and seed-grown zairai bushes in mountain gardens
processing: Steamed only briefly (roughly 20–30 seconds, shorter than standard sencha), then kneaded and rolled into tight, whole needles and dried; the leaf stays intact and the volatile aroma is preserved.
harvest_season: First flush only for the serious lots, picked in May in the mountain districts, which bud later than the lowlands; a little second flush goes into everyday grades.
appearance_dry: Long, intact, tightly rolled needles of dark green with a sheen and almost no dust.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold-green and clear enough to see the bottom of the cup.
appearance_wet: Whole leaves that open out recognisably, bright green with intact edges.
taste_profile: High, fresh aroma, a lighter body with a cleaner, sharper astringency, floral or citrus-peel notes in good mountain lots and a lingering sweetness.

brewing.notes: Whole leaf needs a longer first steep than deep-steamed tea, 60–90 seconds at 70–75 °C. A standard mesh kyusu is fine because the liquor is clear. Worth a fourth steep with hotter water.

vintage_note: A first-flush (ichibancha) tea sold as the current year's harvest, often from a single mountain garden and labelled with the district (Kawane, Honyama, Tenryū, Uji, Yame); the early lots are sold as shincha in May and the rest through the year. It keeps a little better than deep-steamed sencha because the leaf is whole, but it is still meant to be drunk within the year, sealed and cold.
description:
Asamushi is the light-steamed end of sencha, 20–30 seconds in the steamer instead of the usual 30–40 or the deep-steamed minute-plus, and it is the traditional style of the mountain districts: Kawane, Honyama and Tenryū in Shizuoka, Uji in Kyoto, the hills of Yame in Fukuoka. Mountain leaf grows more slowly, thinner and more aromatic, and it does not need the long steam that tames thick lowland leaf.

Short steaming keeps the leaf intact, and the rolling then produces the classic long, tight needle. Because less of the aroma is cooked away, these teas smell of fresh grass, flowers, sometimes citrus peel; the cup is clear enough to see the bottom of the bowl and the body is lighter. The trade-off is structure: the astringency is more visible, and the tea is less forgiving of careless brewing than a deep-steamed one.

Brew it with patience. Whole leaves release slowly, so the first steep wants 60–90 seconds at 70–75 °C, the second a quick pour, and a third and fourth with hotter water are genuinely worth having. The usual mistake is the mirror image of the fukamushi mistake: people steep too briefly, get thin tea, then overcorrect with hot water and get bitterness. Cooler water and more time is the answer. The aroma rises off the cup as it cools, so do not rush it.

This is a tea of small farms and specialist shops rather than supermarkets, usually sold as a single-district or single-garden lot with the district on the label and sometimes 'asamushi' or 'futsumushi' as a style note. Prices run higher than deep-steamed tea from the same year because mountain yields are low and the sorting is careful; seed-grown (zairai) bushes and aromatic cultivars such as Kōshun turn up here more than anywhere else, and the hand-rolled teas entered in the national competitions are nearly always this style.

If you want to understand what steaming does, drink an asamushi and a fukamushi from the same region and year side by side.
